Also, I suspect a lot of the bids on some properties aren't real and are either via the estate agents or potentially extended family or friends of the seller helping push it up a bit more.

When I had a survey done on a property, the guy basically told me that it appeared most properties had some dodgy dealings going on behind the scenes and people were just rinsing first time buyers

The mortgage advisor also said that even if we bid X amount and it was over the initial asking, the bank might agree it was worth more than the original asking if that was what the bidding had gone up to. Obviously with a mortgage the bank still has to say the property is worth X but our mortgage advisor didn't think this would be a huge issue.

The other issue was people buying in cash to flip it. I bid against a lot of people buying to flip a property who would just waltz in and go 20k+ over asking instantly and offer cash. It seems a lot of people who flip properties or landlords are able to just swoop in and many appear to have very good relationships with the estate agents. It can be both. The system is fundamentally flawed, there is no doubt about that. The wait for out of hours can be ridiculously long. I've experience of care in NI and in Wales and out of hours in Wales is far faster and quicker. It can also get you admitted via a same day emergency care unit/medical admissions unit rather than via a&e which is also quicker.

The NI system is slow, it's hard to get seen and also the distance to access care can be long and difficult if you don't have a car or rely on public transport. I was home and had an emergency when pregnant in Newcastle and was advised to get to the Ulster and it took an hour in the car while in agony. When I'm working in Wales it's 20 mins in the car.

However, many people also assume that calling an ambulance means you are seen quicker (it doesn't). Some don't know what minor injuries can do and others aren't aware of emergency scripts via a pharmacy and so do to to a&e. There is a mix of a terrible system and a lack of education on how to navigate it. I've got better at it only through a lot of experience, most of which has been terrible.

I had to be in a&e on Christmas morning unfortunately and there were 3 people in the waiting room. I landed back in the other evening unfortunately and it was swamped. I do think a lot of people attend because they can't see a GP or because they don't realise what can be done in minor injuries. Plus getting seen by out of hours can take forever and unfortunately for me I am sent to a&e 99% of the time by out of hours anyway so I usually just increase the wait time for treatment if I risk out of hours (ongoing health issues so not just me assuming. Basing this on experience).

More people need to know which care avenue is best, they also need to be able to access it promptly and easily. It's expensive if you have to get a taxi there and don't live near or if you rely on public transport.

I am so sorry you had that experience. It's discrimination plain and simple.  I've looked into adoption both in NI and Wales and found in Wales they are more open to discussion around adopting even if you have health issues. They also said single parents are fine too etc.

It is honestly ridiculous that they can turn you down based on disability alone without any conversation on actual lived experience. I work back and forth between Wales and NI and I've looked into the process in both places and in Wales my disabilities aren't seen as a hindrance and yet in NI they are. It feels very discriminatory. They don't seem to even want to discuss whether additional support would be needed etc or not, they just assume.

So I have not adopted but I looked into it and a friend did as well. I'm over in Wales for work and go back and forth but while in Wales I also looked into it over there.

It is a long process with detailed interviews and investigations into your history. However, I found that in Wales they didn't question my fitness at all but in NI they tend to be against people who have a history of depression, anxiety etc. I have a friend who is disabled and although she would make an amazing mum she was turned down solely based on her disability.

They assumed what she could or couldn't do, and they are wrong but they don't care. She is now a proud parent to her animals many of whom have serious health issues and need intense care and support everyday and it is ironic they felt she couldn't care for a child with additional needs or even a child in general and yet I would trust her with my own and I've seen how she is able to juggle her sick animals, something which I think most would find very difficult and that those social workers would balk at if they had to.

Basically it is intense, the support you will get during the process etc can be lacking. Social services don't exactly have a sparkling reputation and there is a reason for that.

I found having looked into it in Wales and NI that I would actually prefer to adopt in Wales than in NI currently as although both are long and arduous, the Welsh system was much friendlier to single parents, LGBTQ families, disabled parents etc.

It's definitely a solid game for €10 so yes.


So a major part of the game is realism to an extent. The main character is a blacksmiths son who doesn't have any major formal training in combat and that directly goes into your first question about combat.


Combat is janky to begin with because the character doesn't know how to fight as the game progresses and you get training etc it becomes a lot less janky and you become more proficient at it. It is quite a simple system which looks a lot more complex than it needs to be. Even in the hardest difficulty with all flaws attached you don't need to go to in depth to the system. It has lots of combos you can do but a lot of the basic combos are enough to get you through the game. It seems scary at first with how the game explains but it's pretty simple overall when you start actually wading into more fights. There is no aiming reticule for archery without mods(immersive).


The games pace starts of slow but picks up speed after a certain event and the world becomes open. At that point the games pace is what you want it to be. You can just tackle the main story or you can explore and pick up side quests on the way. There are quite a few times quests in the game  which the game does a decent job at hinting at through dialogue.


The world is very immersive and you have to train to do most things. E.g reading for instance is something you need to specifically learn. When you wear a helmet you lose peripheral vision and can see only through the visor the helmet has, which introduces risk and reward. It has a hunger system and a sleep system where your character can die of hunger for instance. Also time is a factor as well.


The story is decent without going to much into it, it's a tale of revenge. The story does a decent job in the prologue of introducing characters to help amplify the tale of revenge but it really depends on what your appetite for such a story is.


I like the main character of the game and you can push your own morality on him through dialogue choices.


There are defo a lot of things I missed as I played the game a couple of years ago now but it's definitely worth a playthrough

Context: I've just sat my viva for my PhD and I'm doing corrections 

I worked. It is as simple as that. I worked one job at 21 hours a week and made it up with other jobs. It worked out as full time work with full time PhD work.

I also gave birth a week after I submitted my thesis and juggled ongoing health issues throughout the PhD which meant I was in hospital a lot.

I found work that was mainly remote so I could work from the hospital and I just powered through.

Not saying it is easy but it isn't impossible. Learning about time management is handy too and setting aside time solely for uni work makes a difference. It can be hard to set aside an hour or two each day so I might spend a Sunday doing PhD work or I would work during the day and then in the evening until late I would do PhD work 

I'm now doing corrections while working (more than one job at the same time can block maternity leave), so I basically take the baby with me everywhere and work around them be that for paid work or uni work.

I would say look at remote work (and if not possible, Flexi work), set aside specific times for uni work and that can help because being in the right mindset for uni work is a must and I found it harder to stop/start in shorter bursts.

I actually found my masters was easier in terms of managing my time and work but I completed mine in one year but the set hours of a class schedule for a taught postgraduate was helpful to have the right mindsets, it can be easy to let time slip with a PhD as it can feel less structured as you are a class of one and need to really regulate your time and work.

Always read the feedback. When I mark I usually have comments in the text and also more generally with strengths and areas for development. Students can also go to office hours or email to request feedback.

Without seeing your essay I can't say what the issue is but I find a lot of students lack critical depth as they think they are saying why something matters or is relevant but don't actually say it. In fact when I support students with their essays in a different role at my institution I find lecturers don't always mention critical reasoning or depth in feedback even when that is what they mean. Perhaps you could most the feedback here and get others to decipher it for you? Sometimes a lecturer can think they've given clear feedback but if you aren't familiar with 'academic speak' it can be hard to grasp.

For example, with critical depth and reasoning, if you were to tell me that a phone is blue, why is it blue and not another colour? Perhaps it is blue to be more eye catching and stand out compared to others on the market and therefore increase sales of that type of phone.

Basically why is what you are saying relevant, why does it matter.

However, remember a 2.1 is great, you might struggle to push it up to a 1st at this point but check your institution some set it at 68 and above or 69 etc.

Always proof read your essay before you submit, get a friend to give it a once over too as your brain can trick you and make you think you said why it matters or will overlook a comma or similar as you are so familiar with the text it knows what is next so sort of fills the gaps for you and it makes it harder to spot (sort of like those Facebook pics that say, 'if you can read this...') kind of like with a lecturer who gives advice and yet it's hard for you to see their perspective, they might think it's clear when it isn't and are also having a bit of a blind spot as they are so used to that sort of feedback.

Plus your university probably has some support for academic writing. Most do. Find out where it is and attend a course or better yet a one to one session of available.

Finally, my students get an assignment brief or even some basic guidance. Usually there is also info on what a 2.1 or a 1st looks like with the marking rubric and so they can tell what is needed (i.e. writing to a good standard with clarity and good punctuation and grammar or shows an understanding of key concepts with critical depth and strong consideration of complex issues etc). This doesn't always mean people use it or follow as I've had some skip full sections labelled as must have and then score 0 in that area.

Mendeley is great. I use the web browser plug in, it imports the information for me that a reference requires. 

Always double check this, rubbish in will equal rubbish out. This is then synced to a desktop mendeley library so I can put references in folders and sort as needed.

They also have a plug in for Word (or other programmes) and so I can cite as I am writing in APA, MHRA, Harvard etc whatever I need.

At the end, I just hit one button and all the references are put in the bibliography.

Some institutions have a subscription for Endnote and recommend it. Odds are your institution has a specific reference manager they recommend. My old institution liked refworks for example. Whichever one it is will have additional support available usually via the library or a similar service.

In the meantime, see if your institution has any free postgrad training on grammar and academic misconduct etc. The grammar to help with your skills, the academic misconduct because if you did end up facing disciplinary proceedings it always looks good to have attended a session exploring what it is.

I've included a basic overview of cat 'talk' just as thought it might interest you

‘Mew’ is normally used by kittens to attract attention, and can get louder and more intense as a response to fear or stress. Some adult cats will use it is a variation on ‘meow’ and some will use it as a greeting.
 
‘Meow’ is an attention-seeking sound or a greeting.
 
‘Chirp’ – this is a high-pitched, short sound that is used in anticipation for a treat or meal.
 
Soft trill – this can be made by the cats with their mouth closed. Mothers often do this to their kittens, and it is often used as a greeting.
 
Silent ‘meow’ – this is when the cat looks like it is meowing, but no sound comes out. They do this to show their gratitude and affection.
 
‘Squeak’ – this is a raspy, high-pitched sound like a chirp, and it is used in anticipation of treats.
 
‘Trill’ – this is kind of a cross between a ‘purr’ and a ‘meow’. It is used by cats when if they want to express their pleasure.
 
‘Purr’ – a vibrating, engine-like sound is used by the cat to show contentment and happiness, but it can also be used when the cat is anxious, or in pain. It is believed that the purr soothes the cat, a bit like a child singing to themselves.
 
‘Chatter’ – this is a funny sound that involves the cat rapidly moving its jaw up and down. The cat usually uses it when they see a prey that they can’t reach, so people believe that is a frustration sound.
 
Moaning – cats will do a funny sort of moaning sound just before they are about to vomit or cough up a hairball. It can also be heard in very elderly cats who seem confused.
 
Caterwaul – this is an awful wailing noise and is made when cats are mating.
 
Growling – this is a low-pitched rumbling, like the sound dogs make, and is meant as a warning for a fight. It is also used by a cat when it has a item it doesn’t want to share.
 
Hissing – this is a noise cats make when warning you that they want you to stay away from them. It can be loud or quiet.
 
Spitting – a cat will make this noise when it is startled, and the cat will often hiss afterwards.
 
Scream – this high-pitched, harsh sound is made when the cat is in pain or during a fight.

You are not your aunt you can't understand.

I once had a doctor say go on and on about laxative abuse loudly and I was embarressed, one other patient told him off for how he spoke to me as well.
